# Data Description {#sec-90-data-description}



This appendix documents the modeled market in full. Chapter 2
(@sec-02-notation-and-data-simulated-market) introduces it and says why the book
runs on it; chapter 4 (@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-implementation) measures its
properties. Here we record what each shipped object contains, how it was
constructed, and what it cannot support. Everything below is computed from the
objects as they ship in `tidypm`, so the appendix cannot drift from the data.

The dataset is modeled and contains no real data. Factor models for government
bonds, credit, equities and commodities were estimated by historical simulation
on market data from 1992 to 2022; the factors were replayed, the idiosyncratic
components drawn afresh, and the asset paths reassembled, so that no series is
the history of a real security. The market therefore runs on its own calendar,
model years
1 to 31,
read with the tools of @sec-02-notation-and-data-model-calendar. Its stress
episodes are named for what happens in them and ship as `sim_episodes`. And
because every series is the output of a factor model, the market can be re-run
with its factors shocked, which a history cannot, and
@sec-965-scenario-analysis does so.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
objects <- c("sim_assets",
             "sim_class_returns_monthly", "sim_class_returns_weekly",
             "sim_money_market_monthly", "sim_money_market_weekly",
             "sim_asset_returns_monthly", "sim_asset_returns_weekly",
             "sim_riskfree_monthly", "sim_riskfree_weekly",
             "sim_fx_monthly", "sim_fx_weekly",
             "sim_curve_weekly", "sim_marketcap_weekly",
             "sim_esg_changes_quarterly", "sim_episodes")
# The model years an object covers, from whichever date columns it carries.
years_of <- function(o) {
  x <- get(o)
  d <- do.call(c, unname(as.list(x[intersect(names(x), c("date", "start", "end"))])))
  if (is.null(d)) return("")
  paste(model_year(range(d)), collapse = " to ")
}
inventory <- tibble::tibble(
  object  = objects,
  rows    = vapply(objects, function(o) nrow(get(o)), integer(1)),
  years   = vapply(objects, years_of, character(1)),
  columns = vapply(objects, function(o) paste(names(get(o)), collapse = ", "),
                   character(1))
)
first_week <- min(sim_class_returns_weekly$date)
stopifnot(all(inventory$years[grepl("returns|money_market|fx", objects)] == "1 to 31"),
          first_week - min(sim_riskfree_weekly$date) == 7,
          first_week - min(sim_curve_weekly$date) == 7,
          min(sim_marketcap_weekly$date) < first_week - 7,
          max(sim_marketcap_weekly$date) > max(sim_class_returns_weekly$date))
inventory |>
  kable(align = "lrrl", col.names = c("object", "rows", "model years", "columns"))
```

The return tables and the exchange rates cover model years 1 to 31 exactly. The
weekly bill and the curve start one week before the first weekly return, and
the capitalizations extend past both ends of the sample, so that a lagged
capitalization exists for the first return.

## Class Series {#sec-90-data-description-class-series}

The allocation universe is the sixteen risky class series in
`sim_class_returns_monthly`: five currencies, each with a government bond, a
credit and an equity series, plus one global commodity index. The five
money-market series ship beside them in `sim_money_market_monthly` and are not
part of the universe, for the reason given in
@sec-02-notation-and-data-vocabulary. Both tables carry `date`, `class`,
`return` (a simple total return in decimal) and `index` (a total-return index
with base 100 one period before the first observation).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)
M  <- as_xts_pm(sim_money_market_monthly, date, class, return)
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return
d  <- zoo::index(R)
stopifnot(ncol(R) == 16L, ncol(M) == 5L,
          identical(d, zoo::index(M)),
          all(d == sim_riskfree_monthly$date))

# The index is the compounded return series, in both tables.
rebuilt <- dplyr::bind_rows(sim_class_returns_monthly, sim_money_market_monthly) |>
  dplyr::group_by(class) |>
  dplyr::arrange(date, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(rebuilt = 100 * cumprod(1 + return)) |>
  dplyr::ungroup()
stopifnot(max(abs(rebuilt$rebuilt - rebuilt$index)) < 1e-8)

c(months = nrow(R), first_model_year = min(model_year(d)),
  last_model_year = max(model_year(d)))
#>           months first_model_year  last_model_year 
#>              372                1               31
```
:::

**Weighting.** Equity class series are value-weighted on the market
capitalization of the *previous* weekly observation, so no portfolio is formed
with information it could not have had; government, credit, money-market and
commodity series are equally weighted across their instruments, because no
capitalization exists for them. The portfolio is rebalanced weekly, and the
monthly return is the compounded weekly one, so the monthly series is a
weekly-rebalanced portfolio observed at month ends rather than a
monthly-rebalanced one.

**The money market is a duration asset.** Each `*_money_market` series is the
0.25-year point on a Nelson–Siegel curve fitted to 2-, 5- and 10-year yields,
marked to market. The US series tracks the bill closely but is not the bill:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mm <- as.numeric(M[, "US_money_market"])
c(mm_negative_months   = mean(mm < 0),
  bill_negative_months = mean(rf < 0),
  correlation          = stats::cor(mm, rf))
#>   mm_negative_months bill_negative_months          correlation 
#>             0.188172             0.002688             0.930009
```
:::


Abroad, a three-month instrument has almost no duration, so unhedged in dollars
it is close to a pure currency position:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
vapply(c("EU", "UK", "CH", "JP"), function(rg) {
  fx <- sim_fx_monthly[sim_fx_monthly$region == rg, ]
  stats::cor(as.numeric(M[, paste0(rg, "_money_market")]),
             fx$fx_return[match(zoo::index(M), fx$date)])
}, numeric(1))
#>     EU     UK     CH     JP 
#> 0.9970 0.9953 0.9984 0.9994
```
:::


**Episodes.** Four stress episodes are kept apart throughout the book because
they are economically different. They ship as `sim_episodes`, each named for
what happens in it, and `in_episode()` selects the dates of one, so that no
chapter types a window (@sec-02-notation-and-data-model-calendar).


::: {#tbl-90-episode-windows .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The four named episodes of `sim_episodes` on the model calendar. Each window is a closed interval of dates; the count is of monthly observations.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}

|:-----------------|:------------------|:--------------------------|:--------------------------|------:|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
|`equity_bear`     |equity bear market |April of model year 9      |September of model year 11 |     30|A long decline in equities, led by the most highly valued markets, while the safest government bonds rise.                                |
|`credit_crisis`   |credit crisis      |September of model year 17 |March of model year 18     |      7|A flight to quality: equities and most credit fall together, the safest government bonds rally, and correlations among risky assets rise. |
|`liquidity_shock` |liquidity shock    |February of model year 29  |April of model year 29     |      3|A sudden, short sell-off across every risky class, followed by a fast recovery.                                                           |
|`rates_shock`     |rates shock        |January of model year 31   |December of model year 31  |     12|A rise in yields in which government bonds and credit lose in every region, most equity markets fall, and commodities gain.               |


:::
:::

Every figure is in dollars and unhedged, so a foreign class carries its
currency's move with it. In the equity bear market all five equity
classes fall, the worst by
55%,
while four of the five government
classes gain. In the credit crisis all five equity classes and
four of the five credit classes fall, and
`US_government` gains
8%. The
liquidity shock lasts three
months, in which every equity and credit class and
fourteen of the sixteen classes in all fall.
In the rates shock every government and credit class falls,
together with four of the five equity
classes, and the commodity index gains
12%.

## Instrument Series {#sec-90-data-description-instruments}

`sim_asset_returns_monthly` and `sim_asset_returns_weekly` hold the same market
at instrument level, one column per `asset`, and `sim_assets` describes each
instrument.


::: {#tbl-90-instruments .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Instruments by region and asset class.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|region | equity| government| credit| money_market| commodity|
|:------|------:|----------:|------:|------------:|---------:|
|CH     |     17|          3|      6|            1|         0|
|EU     |     37|          3|      6|            1|         0|
|GLOBAL |      0|          0|      0|            0|         8|
|JP     |     17|          3|      6|            1|         0|
|UK     |     17|          3|      6|            1|         0|
|US     |     35|          3|      6|            1|         0|


:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
Ra <- as_xts_pm(sim_asset_returns_monthly, date, asset, return)
stopifnot(ncol(Ra) == nrow(sim_assets), !anyNA(Ra),
          setequal(colnames(Ra), sim_assets$asset_id))
dim(Ra)
#> [1] 372 181
```
:::


Identifiers are anonymized (`US_EQU_01`, `EU_CRE_03`, `GLOBAL_CMD_02`): a
region, an asset class and a running number. Government bonds are
zero-coupon instruments held at constant maturities of 2, 5 and 10 years; credit
is the same three maturities in two grades (`credit_grade` is `IG` or `HY`); the
money-market instrument is the 0.25-year point on the regional curve; the eight
commodities are a broad index plus gold, energy, precious metals, silver,
agriculture, industrial metals and a crypto series. Equities carry a `sector`.


::: {#tbl-90-sectors .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Equity instruments by sector.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|sector                 | instruments|
|:----------------------|-----------:|
|Financials             |          20|
|Consumer Non-Cyclicals |          18|
|Consumer Cyclicals     |          17|
|Industrials            |          17|
|Healthcare             |          16|
|Technology             |          16|
|Basic Materials        |          12|
|Energy                 |           7|


:::
:::


**Conditioning.** Three maturities per region are priced off a three-factor
curve, and the two credit grades at each maturity share one credit factor, so
some bond combinations are near-exact replicas of others. The instrument-level
covariance is therefore close to singular, which is why every instrument-level
optimization in Part VI needs a constraint or a shrinkage estimator
(@sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory, @sec-21-equity-sleeve-theory).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
ev  <- eigen(stats::cov(Ra), symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
ev16 <- eigen(stats::cov(R), symmetric = TRUE, only.values = TRUE)$values
condition <- c(instruments_log10_condition = log10(max(ev) / min(ev)),
               classes_log10_condition     = log10(max(ev16) / min(ev16)))
stopifnot(min(ev) > 0)                # positive definite, but only just
condition
#> instruments_log10_condition     classes_log10_condition 
#>                      12.196                       4.105
```
:::


## Risk-Free Rate and Exchange Rates {#sec-90-data-description-rates}

`sim_riskfree_monthly` and `sim_riskfree_weekly` are a three-month Treasury
bill carried onto the model's grid: `rate_annual` is the quoted annual rate and
`return` the simple return over one period. The bill enters the model as an
input, and it is the risk-free rate everywhere in the book
(@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(annualized = ann_ret(rf), negative_months = sum(rf < 0),
  min_rate = min(sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual),
  max_rate = max(sim_riskfree_monthly$rate_annual))
#>      annualized negative_months        min_rate        max_rate 
#>         0.02262         1.00000        -0.00010         0.06190
```
:::


`sim_fx_monthly` and `sim_fx_weekly` hold, for the four non-US regions, the
value of one unit of local currency in dollars (`rate`, weekly only) and its
return `fx_return`. Like the bill, the exchange rates enter the model as
inputs. The quote direction matters: a positive `fx_return` means
the local currency appreciated against the dollar, which is a gain for an
unhedged dollar investor holding the local asset. Subtracting `fx_return` from
an unhedged local return gives the hedged return, which is how the book hedges
(@sec-04-descriptive-analysis-application).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sim_fx_monthly |>
  dplyr::group_by(region) |>
  dplyr::summarise(ann_vol = ann_vol(fx_return),
                   ann_return = ann_ret(fx_return), .groups = "drop")
#> # A tibble: 4 × 3
#>   region ann_vol ann_return
#>   <chr>    <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1 CH      0.103     0.0122 
#> 2 EU      0.0953   -0.00907
#> 3 JP      0.101    -0.00171
#> 4 UK      0.0915   -0.0142
```
:::


`sim_curve_weekly` holds the drivers of the bond block: Nelson–Siegel level,
slope and curvature for each region, plus an investment-grade and a high-yield
credit spread per region. Chapter 22 (@sec-22-fixed-income-sleeve-theory)
decomposes bond returns on them.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sort(unique(sim_curve_weekly$series))
#>  [1] "CH_Curvature" "CH_HY_Spread" "CH_IG_Spread" "CH_Level"     "CH_Slope"    
#>  [6] "EU_Curvature" "EU_HY_Spread" "EU_IG_Spread" "EU_Level"     "EU_Slope"    
#> [11] "JP_Curvature" "JP_HY_Spread" "JP_IG_Spread" "JP_Level"     "JP_Slope"    
#> [16] "UK_Curvature" "UK_HY_Spread" "UK_IG_Spread" "UK_Level"     "UK_Slope"    
#> [21] "US_Curvature" "US_HY_Spread" "US_IG_Spread" "US_Level"     "US_Slope"
```
:::


`sim_marketcap_weekly` holds the market capitalization of the
123 equities on the weekly grid,
which is what a capitalization-weighted benchmark needs
(@sec-24-benchmarks-and-active-risk-application, @sec-21-equity-sleeve-implementation).

`sim_esg_changes_quarterly` holds changes in an ESG rating of the equities: the
quarter end (`date`), the instrument (`asset`) and an integer `esg_change`. It
carries changes only, no starting level, and the changes have no effect on the
returns.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
esg <- sim_esg_changes_quarterly
stopifnot(all(esg$asset %in% sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]))
c(changes = nrow(esg), equities = dplyr::n_distinct(esg$asset),
  quarters = dplyr::n_distinct(esg$date),
  first_model_year = min(model_year(esg$date)),
  last_model_year = max(model_year(esg$date)),
  smallest = min(esg$esg_change), largest = max(esg$esg_change),
  share_upgrades = round(mean(esg$esg_change > 0), 2))
#>          changes         equities         quarters first_model_year 
#>          1113.00           122.00            79.00            11.00 
#>  last_model_year         smallest          largest   share_upgrades 
#>            31.00            -4.00             5.00             0.65
```
:::


## Known Limitations {#sec-90-data-description-limitations}

The dataset is frozen at version 6.2.0. The idiosyncratic components of every
instrument are one draw, so a regenerated export is a different realized path
rather than an update, and every number in this book is pinned to this one. The
limitations below are properties of the model and are stated rather than
repaired.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
equity_ids <- sim_assets$asset_id[sim_assets$asset_class == "equity"]
equity_vol <- stats::quantile(apply(Ra[, equity_ids], 2, ann_vol), c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))

overlay    <- 0.03
overlay_se <- overlay / (ann_vol(as.numeric(R[, "EU_equity"])) / sqrt(nrow(R) / 12))

# Share of variance the currency hedge removes from each foreign bond class.
foreign_bonds <- grep("^(UK|EU|CH|JP)_(government|credit)$", colnames(R), value = TRUE)
hedge_share <- vapply(foreign_bonds, function(s) {
  fx <- sim_fx_monthly[sim_fx_monthly$region == sub("_.*$", "", s), ]
  stopifnot(all(fx$date == d))
  u <- as.numeric(R[, s])
  1 - stats::var(u - fx$fx_return) / stats::var(u)
}, numeric(1))
stopifnot(overlay_se < 1, length(foreign_bonds) == 8L, all(hedge_share > 0.5))

round(c(equity_vol, overlay_in_se = overlay_se,
        hedge_share_min = min(hedge_share), hedge_share_max = max(hedge_share)), 2)
#>             25%             50%             75%   overlay_in_se hedge_share_min 
#>            0.26            0.31            0.37            0.79            0.63 
#> hedge_share_max 
#>            0.92
```
:::


- **One realized path.** The factor paths are fixed; only the idiosyncratic
  components are drawn. The market as shipped is one path, not a distribution
  over paths: its factors can be shocked (@sec-965-scenario-analysis), but the
  data hold no second draw of them.
- **The euro-area equity overlay.** Every euro-area equity carries an
  expected-return overlay of three percentage points a year, added as a
  constant weekly drift. It is a stated capital-market assumption,
  0.8 standard errors of the sample mean, made so
  that the class is not excluded by every mean-variance optimizer on the
  sample. No other series carries one.
- **Single securities.** The equity series are individual securities with a
  median volatility of 31 percent,
  half of them between 26 and
  37 percent, and their
  idiosyncratic components are drawn independently. A portfolio of them
  diversifies more readily than a real index would.
- **Currency.** Everything is in dollars, unhedged. For a non-US bond the
  currency is the larger part of the risk, between
  63 and
  92 percent of the variance of the
  eight foreign bond classes, and `sim_fx_*` exists so
  that the hedged position can always be formed.
- **Near rank deficiency.** The bond block is nearly rank-deficient at
  instrument level: the covariance matrix of the 181 instruments has
  a condition number of
  $10^{12.2}$.
  Unconstrained mean-variance on all of them produces nonsense, which is worth
  demonstrating rather than preventing.
- **Derived Swiss credit.** No Swiss credit series with usable history exists,
  so the Swiss credit loadings are derived from the other regions rather than
  measured.
- **No fundamentals, no ESG levels.** The dataset carries no firm fundamentals,
  and of ESG ratings only the 1113 changes of
  `sim_esg_changes_quarterly`, not the levels, so cumulating them gives a
  rating up to an unknown constant. Chapter 20 (@sec-20-sustainability-theory)
  and the value-factor material of Part VI therefore work with what returns,
  capitalizations and rating changes can support.
- **Nominal only.** There is no inflation series; the book works in nominal
  dollars throughout (@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory).
